a.summary: `@Deprecated(forRemoval = true)` on an ABSTRACT interface method forces a compiler warning on every implementor that they cannot avoid, and the method cannot actually be removed without a second source-incompatible break of `Transaction`.
a.failure_scenario:
(a) Warning every implementor must eat. `void sign(SequencedCollection<Signer> signers)` is abstract, so a third-party `Transaction` MUST declare it. javac enables `[removal]` by default (unlike `deprecation`) and fires it on an override, not just a call. I confirmed this with javac 25.0.2 on a minimal repro and on this repo: compiling sava-core's main source set at 1dded1d^ gives 0 warnings; at 1dded1d it gives
  BaseTransaction.java:183: warning: [removal] sign(SequencedCollection<Signer>) in Transaction has been deprecated and marked for removal
  BaseTransaction.java:189: warning: [removal] sign(SequencedCollection<Signer>,byte[],int,int,int) in Transaction has been deprecated and marked for removal
A consumer whose build uses `-Werror` (or Gradle `options.compilerArgs.add("-Werror")`, common in library projects) stops compiling on upgrade at their own `@Override public void sign(SequencedCollection<Signer>)`. Their only escapes are annotating their override `@Deprecated` — which propagates the warning to all of their callers — or `@SuppressWarnings("removal")`. This commit added neither annotation anywhere: not on BaseTransaction.java:183, not on PreV1InterfaceShapeTests.java:70, not on SigningCountTests.java:540.
(b) The removal is not reachable additively. `signInOrder(SequencedCollection)` at :845 holds no implementation — the implementation lives in each implementor's override of the method being removed. Delete :784 and :845's body has nothing to call, so `signInOrder(SequencedCollection)` must become abstract. Adding an abstract method to `Transaction` is precisely the break `PreV1InterfaceShapeTests` exists to prevent (its class javadoc: "Everything v1 added to those interfaces must therefore arrive as a `default`... adding an abstract method without one stops this file compiling, which is the published-library rule enforced by the compiler"). So the `forRemoval = true` at :784 schedules a break the repo's own compatibility pin forbids.

b.summary: `@Deprecated(forRemoval = true)` is applied to the abstract `sign(SequencedCollection<Signer>)`, which implementors cannot stop implementing; honoring the removal later silently rebinds `signInOrder(SequencedCollection)`'s body from positional to by-key signing rather than failing to compile.
b.failure_scenario: Two concrete failures. (a) Today: a third-party implementor sees `[removal] sign(SequencedCollection<Signer>) in Transaction has been deprecated and marked for removal`, deletes the override as instructed, and gets `error: MyTx is not abstract and does not override abstract method sign(SequencedCollection<Signer>)`. There is no way to comply — the warning is unactionable, and MIGRATION.md's closing paragraph ("New instance methods have defaults, so existing Transaction implementations do not need additional method overrides") addresses only the additions and never mentions the deprecated abstract method they are forced to keep. (b) At the promised removal: line 846's unchanged body `sign(signers)` still compiles, because `SequencedCollection<Signer>` is a `Collection<Signer>`, and silently retargets to the by-key `sign(Collection)`. I verified this — with the `SequencedCollection` overload deleted, javac emits `invokeinterface sign:(Ljava/util/Collection;)V` with no error and no warning. `signInOrder` would then sign by public key while its javadoc at 838-843 still promises "the first signer writes the first signature slot regardless of its public key". Notably, the sibling bodies at 851/856/861/866/871 would all fail to compile on removal, so this is the one entry point whose breakage is silent.

instructions.question: How does the defect described by `b` relate to the defect described by `a`?
instructions.focus: Compare the defects, not the wording. Two findings about the same code can still be different defects.

criteria: Different defects: fixing the defect `a` describes would leave the defect `b` describes unfixed, even when both sit in the same code.
The same underlying defect, but `b` narrows it, re-scopes which instances or inputs it covers, or reports it at a different place. Not a different defect in adjacent code.
The same defect restated in different words: fixing one fixes the other.
